prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads moisture levels from a DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 (analog resistive) using an MCP3008 ADC connected on the SPI0 hardware bus, with CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM); the sensor’s analog output is wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0), and the program must sample once per second, logging the raw 10‑bit ADC value (0‑1023) to the console together with a timestamp, while providing robust error handling for any SPI initialization or transfer failures, ensuring that the SPI handle is closed and the driver library is terminated cleanly on all exit paths, and supporting graceful shutdown when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the current from an MLX91219 Hall‑Effect Current Sensor (analog output) using an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1, with the sensor’s ADDR pin tied to GND, the sensor’s analog output connected to ADS1115 channel AIN0, SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM); configure the ADS1115 for single‑shot mode, single‑ended input on AIN0 (MUX = 100), a programmable gain of ±4.096 V and a data rate of 128 SPS, then every 500 ms read the 16‑bit conversion result using the appropriate API call with correct byte order, convert it to amperes, and log the current value to the console, while gracefully handling any I2C write or read errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT the program closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads a Honeywell/SGX MICROceL MICS-4514 CO sensor (dual‑element MOS, NO2/CO) via I2C bus 1, using an external 16‑bit ADC such as an ADS1115 or a simulated 16‑bit raw reading, converts the raw CO resistance value to a concentration in ppm with a calibrated logarithmic curve, and logs each timestamped ppm value to a file named co_log.txt every 5 seconds; the program must verify successful driver library initialization, creation of the I2C handle, and detect any I2C read failures that indicate a missing sensor or bus error, and it must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY‑026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO 4 (BCM) for flame presence, routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0, and connecting the MCP3008 chip‑select to CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM) with SCLK on GPIO 11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO 10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO 9 (BCM); the program must log once per second to a timestamped CSV file named flame_data.csv containing the flame presence flag (1/0) and a temperature reading, must validate driver library initialization, SPI handle creation, each SPI transfer, and all file I/O, skipping any entry and printing an error to stderr when the sensor is absent or a SPI bus error occurs, and must cleanly release all resources on normal exit and on SIGINT (Ctrl‑C), using the driver library for all GPIO and SPI operations and not employing any other software library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the SGX Sensortech MICS-4514 dual MOS sensor (CO/NO2) over the I2C bus, extracts the two 16‑bit ADC readings (OX for CO and RED for NO2) from the four‑byte response, converts the OX value to a CO concentration in ppm, and every 5 seconds appends the CO ppm value to a file named co_log.txt while also checking whether the value meets or exceeds a 25 ppm alert threshold and, if so, writing an alert entry to a separate file named alert_log.txt; the program must include robust error handling for I2C initialization failures, read errors, and any file‑I/O problems, and must ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, thereby simulating an industrial air‑quality monitoring system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads sound pressure levels from two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU analog MEMS microphones, using a bit‑banged I2C emulation on bus 1 with the analog OUT signals connected to GPIO2/BCM2 and GPIO3/BCM3, samples each microphone every 100 ms, computes the average level, and appends a timestamped entry of that average to a file named audio_log.txt; if a read from either sensor fails the program must log an error value of –999.0 dB for that sample and continue operation, and it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing all I2C handles and terminating the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples audio from two Analog Devices ADMP401 MEMS microphones using an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0, with chip‑select lines CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) and CE1 on GPIO9 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), and SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM), while driving an LED on GPIO27 (BCM); the program must acquire one sample from each microphone every 1 ms for a total window of 100 ms (100 samples per channel), compute the RMS level for each channel, log the window timestamp together with mic1 RMS and mic2 RMS to a file named audio_events.csv, trigger the LED to stay on for 500 ms whenever either RMS exceeds a high‑level threshold, include error handling for SPI initialization failures and file I/O errors, and cleanly handle a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by turning the LED off and releasing all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples the analog output of a Melexis MLX91204 Hall effect current sensor using an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO2 BCM, SCL on GPIO3 BCM), reading single‑ended on channel A0 at a rate of 10 Hz, converting the raw values to current, storing each converted reading in a circular buffer of 100 elements, and triggering a warning LED on GPIO17 BCM whenever the average of the buffered currents exceeds a 50.0 A threshold; the implementation must employ the driver library I2C API functions for raw register operations, include robust error handling for driver initialization, I2C reads, and sensor‑absent conditions, and handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off the LED and releases all resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Adafruit TCS34725 I2C color sensor on I2C bus 1, initializing the sensor through the supplied driver, waiting at least 3 ms after power‑on before any read, then reading the clear, red, green and blue values once every second and appending a line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,clear,red,green,blue” to a file named color_log.csv, creating the file with a header row if it does not already exist; the program must check the return value of every I2C read and write, printing a warning to stderr on a transient failure and continuing, but if three consecutive I2C operations fail it should exit gracefully, and it must exit with a non‑zero code if the driver initialization or I2C open fails or if the sensor’s ID register does not match the expected value; on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the program must close the I2C handle, flush and close the CSV file, and invoke the driver’s cleanup call, and it must implement the one‑second interval without using a blocking sleep that would prevent signal handling.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that sequentially activates and deactivates four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relay modules connected as a light sequencer on the GPIO digital output bus, using BCM pins 17, 22, 23, and 24 for relays 1‑4 respectively; the program must initially set all relay pins to inactive (LOW, assuming active‑high relays), then in an infinite loop activate each relay for one second, deactivate it, wait one second before moving to the next relay, and repeat this pattern indefinitely, while checking the result of every driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, etc.) for errors, providing clear comments throughout, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that, on exit, deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines; no SPI, ADC, temperature sensor, or logging functionality may be used and only standard C libraries together with the driver library may be employed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the analog output of a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over the SPI bus CE0 on GPIO 8 using mode 0 at 1 MHz, sampling every 10 ms, and when the measured value exceeds a defined threshold it must turn on an LED wired to GPIO 16 (BCM) for 500 ms, log the event with a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” to a file named sound_events.log, apply a debounce delay after each trigger, and gracefully handle any SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selections, or GPIO initialization errors by checking all driver library calls and file operations; the program must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt cleanly releases resources by closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver library, and turning off the LED, and it must be written using the driver library, not the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the analog output of a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor through an MCP3008 on SPI channel 0 configured at 1 MHz mode 0, polls the sensor once per second, appends the rain level together with a timestamp to a file named rain_log.txt (flushing after each write), and based on a default rain‑threshold value of 5 decides whether to close or open a window: when the measured level exceeds the threshold the program must drive a motor forward for exactly three seconds using the L298N‑based DC motor driver with IN1 connected to GPIO17 (BCM), IN2 to GPIO18 (BCM) and ENA (PWM) to GPIO27 (BCM) at a PWM duty of 150 within a range of 255, otherwise it must drive the motor in reverse for three seconds; the window is assumed initially open; the code must check every initialization, system call and I/O return value, handling failures to initialize the driver library, open the SPI device or the log file by printing clear error messages and performing proper cleanup, and must also detect and log any SPI transfer or file‑write errors without crashing; signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM must set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag that causes the main loop to stop the motor, close the SPI interface, close the log file and terminate the driver library before exiting, and all resources must be released on any exit path; the program should be compiled with gcc -o rain rain.c -lthe driver library -lrt -lpthread.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors the analog output of a MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier with automatic gain control using a bit‑banged ADC sampling on BCM GPIO26, detects a clap event, and when a valid clap is recognized (respecting a 50 ms debounce interval) turns on an LED connected to BCM GPIO16 for 500 ms while printing a timestamped detection message to the console; the implementation must verify that the ADC driver and GPIO mode settings are successfully initialized, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and include a SIGINT handler that, on Ctrl + C, turns off the LED and cleanly releases all resources, all written in C11 without using any deprecated APIs and running until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads the Sharp GP2Y0A21YK0F IR distance sensor, which for this exercise is connected as a digital input on GPIO17 (BCM) via the GPIO digital input bus, treating the analog output as a binary 0 or 1 value; the program must log each read to a file named distance_log.txt in append mode with a timestamp formatted as YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, print “Feeder Activated” to the console when the sensed distance is less than 200 mm and “Feeder Idle” otherwise, handle any errors opening or reading the GPIO file by printing an error message and retrying after a one‑second delay, retry after one second on any other error, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the program cleanly unexports GPIO17 and exits, running indefinitely until interrupted while noting that a real implementation would require an ADC such as an MCP3008 but the current requirement treats the sensor as a digital input.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on the SPI bus (CE0, SCLK = GPIO11, MOSI = GPIO10, MISO = GPIO9) using single‑ended channel 0, samples the moisture level every 60 seconds, converts the ADC value to a moisture percentage, and activates a 12 V submersible water pump connected to a relay on GPIO17 (BCM) when the percentage falls below a defined threshold, logging each sample to a file named soil_moisture.log with a timestamp, the moisture percentage, and the pump status (ON or OFF); the program must verify successful initialization of the SPI interface, the ADC, and the log file, handle sensor read failures gracefully, validate ADC readings, and on receipt of SIGINT perform a graceful shutdown that turns the pump off, closes the log file, and releases all GPIO resources, while respecting the constraint that the relay is active‑high and no external driver library or similar software component is used, relying only on modern APIs provided by the system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the DRV5055‑A1 Hall‑effect sensor through an external MCP3008 ADC over the SPI bus /dev/spidev0.0 configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, sampling the sensor voltage on MCP3008 channel 0 every 500 ms, converting the raw integer reading to magnetic field strength using integer arithmetic and printing the result with two decimal places, and appending a CSV line “<unix_epoch>,<B_mt_two_decimals>” to a file named magnetic_log.txt; the MCP3008 VDD and VREF must be tied to the 3.3 V rail, its DOUT line to GPIO10 (BCM), DIN to GPIO9 (BCM), CLK to GPIO11 (BCM), and CS/SHDN to GPIO8 (gpiochip0 line 8) (BCM), while the DRV5055‑A1 VCC is also powered from 3.3 V and its VOUT is connected to the ADC channel 0, and the program must include standard headers such as stdint.h, check the return value of every open, ioctl, SPI transfer, fopen and fprintf call propagating errors, log any ADC read failure to stderr, skip that sample and continue, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing the GPIO line, closing the SPI file descriptor, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si1102 proximity sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, configures the sensor’s proximity interrupt to GPIO27 (BCM numbering) on a rising edge, and on each interrupt reads the 16‑bit proximity value, compares it to a threshold (default 1000 but overrideable with a command‑line option “‑t <threshold>”), and appends a line to a file named proximity.log containing the current timestamp in “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” format, the raw proximity reading, and the status string “SAFE” if the value is less than or equal to the threshold or “ALERT” if it exceeds the threshold; the program must also accept an optional “‑a <i2c_address>” argument to set the I2C address in hex or decimal, must initialise the I2C interface and GPIO with full error checking, must verify every I2C transaction, GPIO setup, and file operation and print any errors to stderr, must implement a thread‑safe interrupt handler that does not perform blocking calls (using a flag or queue to defer processing), and must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt cleanly shuts down by closing the I2C device, closing the log file, and terminating the sensor driver, while using the provided driver facilities for GPIO and I2C but not for higher‑level sensor handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor and drives an 8‑ohm speaker as a theremin‑like instrument, using the hardware‑timed PWM on PWM0 (GPIO18, BCM) to generate audio tones whose pitch is controlled by the measured distance; the HC‑SR04 trigger line must be pulsed for 10 µs on GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line read on GPIO24 (BCM) with a timeout of 200 ms, mapping distances from 2 cm to 200 cm to frequencies between 200 Hz and 2000 Hz on a logarithmic scale with a 50 % duty cycle, while performing robust error checking on every driver API call and, if a distance is out of range or a timeout occurs, preserving the previous frequency, and installing a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops the PWM and terminates the driver, ensuring all resources are released on exit.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35‑DIS‑B sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented single‑shot high‑repeatability measurement command with clock‑stretching disabled, waiting at least 15 ms after issuing the command before reading the six‑byte result, sampling every five seconds, validating both CRC‑8 checksums with the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging each reading to a CSV file named environment.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by temperature in Celsius and relative humidity in percent, inserting a header row if the file does not already exist or is empty; the program must check the driver initialization, opening of the I2C bus, every I2C read/write operation, CRC validation, and file opening, printing a descriptive error to stderr on any failure and either continuing or exiting as appropriate, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that performs a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the sensor library’s shutdown call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 temperature and humidity sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3) using the documented I2C address, polling each measurement until data is available or a 100 ms timeout expires, reading three bytes (MSB, LSB, CRC) for each value and verifying the CRC‑8 checksum with the documented polynomial and initial value, logging a line every 5 seconds to a CSV file named environment.log with a header “timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent” and ISO‑8601 timestamps, writing “ERROR” in place of the numeric fields together with a descriptive message to stderr whenever an I2C or CRC error occurs, checking the return value of every system call, handling sensor‑absent conditions such as I2C open failure or NACK, and on any read failure issuing the documented sensor reset command before the next cycle; the program must also install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and exits gracefully, thereby simulating a greenhouse monitoring system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, initiates continuous measurement with the documented command, waits the required conversion time, then reads the 9‑byte response containing pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC and three scale‑factor bytes, validates the CRC‑8 for both pressure and temperature raw values, converts the raw data to floating‑point pressure (Pa) and temperature (°C), and logs each sample once per second to a binary file named airflow.dat with pressure followed by temperature as floats while keeping the file handle open across samples; the program must check driver initialization, I2C opening, command write and read results, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and implement signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, terminates the driver, and closes the file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, sends the documented continuous measurement command, waits the documented conversion time of 45 ms, then reads the 9‑byte response (three data words each followed by a CRC‑8 byte) and validates each CRC‑8 with the documented polynomial; the program must log each pressure reading together with a timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt every 5 seconds, handle any I2C write or read errors, CRC failures, or the sensor being absent without crashing, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate the driver library gracefully for use in a DIY ventilation system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the differential pressure from a Honeywell Zephyr HAF Series HAFBLF0100A2AX5 digital airflow sensor over the I2C bus, samples the sensor every 100 ms, computes the corresponding flow rate, and drives a PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM numbering) using hardware PWM at a frequency of 25 kHz, while logging each measurement to a file named flow_log.txt in the format “timestamp,pressure_Pa\n”; the program must include robust handling of I2C communication failures by logging errors to stderr without crashing, and must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning off the fan, closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads pressure and temperature from an STMicroelectronics LPS33HW pressure sensor on the I2C bus, sampling once per second using the sensor’s API call, and logs each reading to a file named environmental_data.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX hPa, Temperature: XX.XX °C” by converting the current time with localtime_r; the program must check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, and on any failure write a timestamped error message to both stderr and the log file while continuing the loop, flush the log file after each write, and handle graceful termination on SIGINT by setting a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, then closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the temperature from an STLM75 digital temperature sensor on the I2C bus once per second, stores each reading in a 10‑element circular buffer in memory and computes a running average, then drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) so that the LED is turned on when the average temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off otherwise; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, that the I2C bus can be opened, and that each I2C read succeeds, skipping any iteration where a failure occurs, and it must handle SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the LED off, closing the I2C handle and invoking the library’s cleanup call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads CO₂, temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SCD30 CO₂ sensor on the I2C bus, samples the data every 5 seconds, and writes each sample to an air_quality.log file as a CSV line containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp followed by CO₂ in ppm, temperature in °C and humidity in %RH, flushing the log after each write; the program must implement ventilation control logic where CO₂ below 800 ppm results in an OFF state, between 800 ppm and 1199 ppm a LOW state, and 1200 ppm or above a HIGH state, and must robustly handle driver library initialization failures, I2C open/write/read errors, sensor non‑response, data‑not‑ready conditions and CRC mismatches by logging the error and continuing without crashing; a sigaction handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must stop the periodic measurement, close the I2C handle, close the log file and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting, and when the program is run in a mocked or emulated environment with no hardware it should log the lack of sensor access and exit gracefully with return code 0 rather than aborting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over the I2C bus, using a default sampling interval of 1000 ms that can be overridden with a command‑line argument, and prints each reading to the console with a timestamp; each reading must consist of exactly nine bytes – pressure MSB, pressure LSB, pressure CRC‑8, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC‑8, scale‑factor MSB, scale‑factor LSB, scale‑factor CRC‑8 – and the program must verify the CRC‑8 for the pressure, temperature, and scale‑factor words, handle I2C failures robustly by detecting sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, emit a clear diagnostic message and exit if the sensor is not connected, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by installing appropriate signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that the program terminates with exit code 0 on those signals while still exiting with an error code on unrecoverable I2C errors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads temperature from a Silicon Labs Si7051 temperature sensor connected via I2C on bus 1, using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), logging the measured temperature in degrees Celsius to the console every 5 seconds, with robust handling of I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the absolute pressure from a Melexis MLX90833 sensor over the I2C bus, logging the pressure value to the console together with a timestamp every 500 ms; the program must verify that all driver initialization steps succeed and must check the result of every I2C read and write operation, handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and it must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that on any exit path all resources are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads temperature and pressure from a TDK ICP‑10101 barometric pressure sensor on the I2C bus, triggering a measurement, waiting 7 ms, then reading the results in a loop that repeats every 5 seconds; each successful read must be printed to stdout with an ISO‑8601 timestamp such as “2024-01-15T14:30:00 - Temperature: 22.45 C, Pressure: 101325.00 Pa”, while every I2C driver call’s return value must be checked and a sensor‑absent condition detected when a read returns a negative value or all bytes match the documented default, logging an error message to stderr without terminating the program; the application must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s cleanup call on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that periodically reads pressure from a Melexis MLX90819 digital I2C version pressure sensor over the I2C bus at a 1‑second sampling interval, prints each reading to stdout prefixed with a timestamp, handles any I2C communication failures such as read/write errors or a missing sensor by printing an appropriate message to stderr while continuing operation, and installs a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that exits cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor after ensuring the device was opened with proper error handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces over I2C to a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa differential pressure sensor using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM, bus 1) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM, bus 1) to monitor HVAC airflow, triggering a measurement then waiting 45 ms before reading exactly 9 bytes (three 2‑byte words each followed by a CRC‑8 byte) and validating each word’s CRC‑8 with the documented polynomial and initial value, logging each successful sample to a file named pressure_log.txt in CSV format containing a timestamp, the differential pressure in pascals and the temperature in degrees Celsius, handling any I2C open, write or read errors and gracefully dealing with the sensor‑absent condition, and ensuring that all resources are properly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal, all within the constraints of a DIY HVAC airflow monitoring application.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800‑500Pa sensor on the I2C bus, waiting at least 8 ms after each trigger before reading the three‑byte response (two data bytes followed by a CRC‑8 byte using the documented polynomial and initial value), verifying the CRC‑8 for each measurement, and logging the timestamped pressure value to a file named airflow_log.csv with a header row added only when the file is newly created; the program must perform error handling on every I2C call, detect and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, include the necessary POSIX headers such as unistd.h to use access() with F_OK, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on normal termination as well as on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads two Analog Devices ADPD105 photometric front‑end sensors on the I2C bus, computes the correlated color temperature (CCT) from the sensor data, and logs the average CCT once per second to a file named cct_log.csv, creating the file with a header line “Timestamp,Average_CCT” if it does not already exist; the implementation must use the sensor’s API calls or equivalent block reads for register access, verify the success of every I2C read and write operation, and on any sensor‑absent or bus‑error condition gracefully log an error to stderr and skip that cycle’s entry, while ensuring that all I2C handles, file streams and any driver resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the absolute pressure and temperature from a Melexis MLX90824 absolute pressure sensor over the I2C bus, performing a read cycle every 2 seconds, and appends each measurement together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt; the program must check the result of every driver library or I2C call, and if the sensor is absent, the bus reports an error, or a read fails, it must log the error with a timestamp instead of silently skipping, and it must ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, SIGINT, and SIGTERM—it cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the sensor library’s cleanup API, while running indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the temperature from an STMicroelectronics LM75B sensor on the I2C bus once every second, stores the last 60 samples in a circular buffer in memory, computes the running average, and drives a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan is turned on when the average exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off when it falls below 26.0 °C; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, opening of the I2C interface, each I2C read, and each GPIO write, logging any failures to stderr and simply retrying on the next cycle without crashing, and it must handle SIGINT or SIGTERM by stopping the fan, closing the I2C handle, and terminating the driver library cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C, waiting 45 ms after issuing the first measurement command before reading, then sampling once every second, reading exactly nine bytes each cycle and validating each CRC using the Sensirion CRC‑8 polynomial and its documented initial value; the program must log each reading to a file named airflow.log in CSV format with columns timestamp, differential pressure (Pa) and temperature (°C), print a warning to stderr whenever the pressure exceeds 5.0 Pa, robustly handle I2C read/write failures, CRC mismatches and the case where the sensor is absent, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle, close the log file and invoke the library’s call() cleanup function.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces two Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors on the GPIO bus, connecting sensor 1 OUT to GPIO23 (BCM), sensor 2 OUT to GPIO24 (BCM), and driving an LED (anode) on GPIO25 (BCM) through a 220‑330 Ω resistor to ground, polling the sensor outputs every 100 ms, turning the LED on immediately when either sensor reads LOW (active‑LOW indicating an obstacle within roughly 10 cm) and turning it off only when both sensors read HIGH, verifying the driver initialization and checking the return code of every library API call, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released via the appropriate library call on every exit path, including handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a conveyor belt using two E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensors connected via GPIO, with sensor 1 OUT wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 OUT wired to GPIO18 (BCM); the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, validate each sensor read, and consider a stall confirmed only when both sensors read LOW (0) continuously for at least 2 seconds, then record a timestamped entry for each confirmed stall in a file named stall_log.txt while avoiding duplicate entries for the same stall event, handling any file I/O errors that may occur, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the process receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with the Texas Instruments TMAG5170‑Q1 I2C 3D Hall‑Effect sensor on I2C bus 1, configures the sensor for continuous‑conversion mode with all three axes enabled and a 50 mT range, then reads the X, Y, and Z magnetic field values every 100 ms in an infinite loop until the user terminates the program with Ctrl‑C, logging each reading to a CSV file named magnetic_log.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and writing a header row if the file is newly created, while checking every I2C read and write return code and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions by printing error messages to stderr and continuing operation, and finally registering a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the CSV file, and invoking the sensor’s library cleanup call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that runs as a daemon and continuously polls the SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to the GPIO bus on pin GPIO23 (BCM numbering), using a pull‑down resistor on the input to keep the line low when dry, reading the sensor every 2 seconds and generating an alert whenever a logic HIGH is detected; on each detection the program must print an alert message to stdout and append a line to a file named flood_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected”, while also checking that the driver library initializes correctly and, if a GPIO read fails, logging an error entry to the same file and scheduling an automatic re‑initialization attempt after 60 seconds; the daemon must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to release all resources cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Bookworm or later that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall‑effect sensor connected to the GPIO bus, with the sensor output wired to physical pin 7 (BCM GPIO4), by configuring the pin as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled and counting rising‑edge pulses using GPIO interrupts; the program must count pulses in a one‑second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, compute the revolutions per minute, and log one sample per second to a file named rpm_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>” while also printing the same line to stdout, flushing the file after each write; it must check every driver‑library call and the file‑open call for errors, exiting with a diagnostic message on failure, but if the sensor is absent or not rotating it should log an RPM of 0 instead of aborting; finally, the program must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall‑effect sensors connected on the GPIO bus in an interrupt‑driven quadrature configuration, with Sensor A wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and Sensor B to GPIO27 (BCM) and hardware pull‑up resistors providing the required 90° electrical offset, to detect the direction of rotation and log each clockwise or counter‑clockwise event to a file named rotation_log.txt using millisecond‑precision timestamps formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.mmm”; the implementation must employ the driver’s edge‑triggered alerts via the library’s API call for interrupt handling (without using any other driver library), maintain a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to infer direction, protect the shared state between the ISR and the main thread with a mutex, have the main loop wait on a condition variable or sleep rather than busy‑wait, check all error paths including each of the three library’s API call() invocations and the file open operation, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by flushing and closing the log file and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the GPIO bus to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B digital capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO23 (physical pin 16, BCM 23) and to drive an LED on GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18) with an appropriate current‑limiting resistor, polling the sensor every 50 ms so that the LED is illuminated only while the sensor is actively touched; the program must open the GPIO chip, request the input line for the sensor and the output line for the LED, check the return status of every driver call including chip opening, line requests, reads and writes, handle the situation where the GPIO chip is unavailable, log startup, shutdown, each touch event and any errors to the system syslog using openlog/syslog, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that perform a graceful shutdown by turning the LED off and releasing all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads touch input from a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) to capture rising‑edge events and toggles an LED attached to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) on each detected touch; the program must employ the line event interface to wait for rising edges rather than polling, apply a software debounce of approximately 50 ms after each rising‑edge detection, initialize the LED line as an output and drive it LOW at startup, verify the result of every driver call (chip open, line request, event wait, read, write) and print clear error messages to stderr when a call fails, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by gracefully releasing all driver resources (lines and chip) before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls two SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensors on the GPIO bus—sensor 1 connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO17 (BCM)—with a 50 ms loop to debounce, drives LED 1 on GPIO27 (BCM) and LED 2 on GPIO22 (BCM) such that each LED is lit while its corresponding sensor is touched (sensors are active‑high digital outputs), records every touch and release event in a 100‑entry in‑RAM circular buffer storing the sensor pin number, a Unix timestamp, and the new state while maintaining an overflow counter, checks the return value of every API call and prints a diagnostic to stderr on any failure, handles SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off both LEDs, calls the required API cleanup function, and on shutdown prints the full contents of the log buffer together with the overflow count to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a Raindrop Sensor Module with a digital output connected to GPIO17 (BCM) on the GPIO bus, enabling the internal pull‑up resistor on that pin so the input is defined when the sensor is disconnected, and polls the pin every 500 ms; the program must detect the active‑low condition where a LOW (0) level indicates rain and a HIGH (1) level indicates no rain, and it should write timestamped “Rain Detected” or “No Rain” messages to /var/log/rain_events.log only when the state changes, while checking the return value of every driver library call and of fopen, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the log file and releases any driver resources on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors a rotating shaft’s RPM by reading two DRV5032FJDBZR Hall‑Effect sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO18 (BCM), applying approximately a 5 ms debounce to each state change, logging every transition to a CSV file named shaft_log.txt in the format “timestamp,sensor1_state,sensor2_state”, printing the calculated RPM to the console, handling any GPIO initialization failures or file I/O errors gracefully, including the standard headers such as errno.h and string.h to ensure clean compilation, and guaranteeing that all resources are released properly on every exit path, including handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform orderly cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads heart rate and SpO2 data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 I2C optical sensor on I2C bus 1, pausing one second between each read, and appends each measurement to a file named biometric_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Heart Rate: X BPM, SpO2: Y%%” while flushing the file after every write; the program must use the driver library for I2C access, check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, print any communication errors to stderr and keep running, and it must also install a SIGINT handler so that when Ctrl‑C is pressed it gracefully shuts down by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and terminating the driver library before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the structural integrity of a miniature bridge model using two digital tilt sensors (Omron D7E-3) connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 on GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 on GPIO18 (BCM), both configured as inputs with internal pull‑down resistors enabled, and drives an alarm (buzzer/LED) on GPIO27 (BCM) which is active‑high and initialized LOW; the program must poll each sensor every 100 ms via the library’s API call, log ISO‑8601 timestamps (YYYY‑MM‑DDTHH:MM:SS) to a file named bridge_integrity.log for tilt‑start, threshold‑exceeded, and tilt‑end events, activate the alarm if either sensor reads HIGH continuously for more than 2 seconds, deactivate the alarm when both sensors return to LOW, include error handling that checks the driver library initialization, the log file opening, and the API call return values, and implement clean shutdown handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivates the alarm, closes the log file, calls the library’s API cleanup, and guarantees the alarm is off on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an Omron D7S‑A0011 seismic sensor on I2C bus 1 using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), polls the sensor every 100 ms, detects earthquake‑like events when the Euclidean vibration magnitude exceeds a threshold of 500, logs each threshold‑exceeding event to a file named seismic_events.log with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the peak vibration value, turns on an alert LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for 1 second for each such event, initializes the sensor by verifying its presence and clearing the power‑down bit in CTRL1, handles I2C communication errors and sensor‑absent conditions with up to three retries per read, and on receipt of Ctrl+C/SIGINT cleanly releases the I2C handle, the driver library, and closes the log file; the program must be built with gcc -O2 -Wall -o seismic seismic.c -lthe driver library -lm -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads obstacle detection data from four Keywish KY‑032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors connected via the GPIO bus, with the sensor OUT pins wired to GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (BCM numbering), and drives an LED on GPIO18 (BCM) such that the LED is turned ON whenever any sensor reports an object (the sensors are active‑low, so a logic 0 indicates detection) and OFF otherwise; the program must poll the four inputs every 50 ms without using blocking delays that would impede prompt signal handling, must robustly handle any GPIO initialization errors such as failures to open the chip or request lines, and must cleanly release all GPIO resources when receiving a SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors five Keyes KY‑026 flame sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with the digital‑output pins of the sensors wired to BCM GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, and 27 (physical pins 3, 5, 7, 11, 13), polling each line once per second and, when a change from HIGH to LOW is observed, performing a 50 ms debounce re‑read to confirm a flame transition; on confirmed detection the program must append a line to “/var/log/flame_events.log” formatted as “<ISO 8601 UTC timestamp> - Sensor ID: <id> (GPIO <pin>) - Flame Detected”, while using syslog with facility LOG_USER and ident “flame_monitor” to report startup, any read‑error per sensor, and shutdown events, checking the result of every driver call for opening the chip, getting a line, requesting a line, and reading a line as well as every file I/O call (fopen, flock, fprintf, fflush) and logging and continuing on per‑sensor read failures but aborting only if the chip cannot be opened or a line cannot be acquired or requested; the program should keep an array of line pointers for the five sensors, install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, and on termination release all requested lines, close the chip, and call closelog() on both normal and error paths, and it must be compiled with gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o flame_monitor flame_monitor.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the eight individual touch states from a TTP226 8‑channel capacitive touch sensor connected via GPIO, using the pins OUT0‑OUT7 mapped to BCM GPIO 5, 6, 13, 19, 26, 12, 16, and 20, and polls all eight pins every 50 ms; the program must log to the console only when a state changes, printing an ISO‑8601 timestamp together with the sensor index (0‑7) and the corresponding BCM pin number and indicating whether a touch was detected or released, must include robust error handling for GPIO chip initialization, line resolution, bulk line requests, and read failures—printing a descriptive error that includes the errno value and exiting with a non‑zero status on unrecoverable errors—and must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl‑C), and must compile cleanly with `gcc -Wall -Wextra -lgpiod` without using any driver‑library v2‑only APIs such as struct the library's API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements an adaptive grow light system using a VEML7700 lux sensor on I2C bus 1 to set the brightness of a grow light LED connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hardware PWM at a 1000 Hz frequency, sampling the ambient light every 1 second, mapping lux readings to PWM duty cycles in the range 0‑100 according to the rule lux < 100 → 100 % brightness, lux < 500 → 75 %, lux < 1000 → 50 %, lux ≥ 1000 → 25 %, writing a line to “grow_log.txt” after each sample that contains an ISO‑8601 timestamp, the measured lux value, the selected brightness level, and an error code, flushing the file after each write, checking and handling errors for driver initialization, opening the I2C bus, configuring the sensor, reading the ambient light sensor, and performing PWM operations, logging and handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus fails, and providing a graceful shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM that turns off the LED, closes the I2C bus, closes the log file, and terminates the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an 8‑channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module over GPIO, reading channels 1‑8 on BCM pins 2‑9 (configured as inputs with pull‑down resistors) and controlling an alert LED on BCM GPIO17 (configured as an output); the program must initialize the driver library and verify success, exiting with an error message on failure, then poll the sensor every 50 ms, debounce each channel so that a single press generates only one log entry, write each touch event to a file named touch_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS – Channel X Touched” (where X is 1‑8), ensure all file I/O operations are checked for errors with diagnostics printed to stderr, turn the LED on whenever any channel transitions from untouched to touched and turn it off only when all channels are released, and install a clean signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turns off the LED, releases the driver library resources, and exits gracefully.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that communicates with an Analog Devices ADIS16266 digital gyroscope over SPI channel 0 using CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) in SPI mode 3 (CPOL = 1, CPHA = 1) at a 1 MHz clock, performing 16‑bit register accesses with a 2‑byte transfer per register and no dummy byte, sending a read command by OR‑ing the register address with bit 7 and receiving the response in the following transaction, verifying the WHO_AM_I register on startup, and then sampling the angular rate at a 10 ms interval, converting the raw value with the scale factor of 0.0305 deg/sec/LSB, and appending timestamped readings to a single CSV file named gyro_log.csv that is opened once at program start with an appropriate header and never reopened; the code must check the return value of every SPI driver call, print informative error messages on any failure, and handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the SPI handle, terminating the driver, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads angular velocity data from a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope on I2C bus 1, sampling every 10 ms, converts the raw values using the 8.75 mdps/LSB sensitivity (divide by 114.285), and appends timestamped records to a file named gyro_log.csv with a header row “Timestamp,X,Y,Z” where timestamps are recorded with nanosecond precision; the program must verify that the sensor’s WHO_AM_I register returns the documented value before proceeding, retry any I2C write during initialization up to three times, check the result of every I2C call and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions appropriately, and on receipt of SIGINT perform graceful termination by closing the I2C handle, closing the CSV file, and invoking the sensor’s library cleanup API.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the digital output (DO) of a KY-026 Flame Sensor Module connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) on the GPIO bus every 500 ms, enables the internal pull‑up resistor on that line because the sensor’s open‑collector output is active‑LOW (LOW indicates flame, HIGH indicates no flame), and writes each reading to an append‑mode file named flame_events.log with an immediately flushed line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS – Flame detected: YES” when the pin reads LOW or “… NO” when it reads HIGH; when a flame is detected the program must also print the message “FLAME DETECTED!” to the console, and it must check that the driver initialization succeeded, verify that the log file handle is valid, and treat any sensor read error (e.g., the API returning PI_BAD_GPIO) by logging an error line instead of a false positive; a SIGINT handler should be installed so that pressing Ctrl‑C sets a flag that cleanly exits the polling loop, and on any exit path the program must close the log file if open and call the library’s cleanup function.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a dual‑factor door‑lock authentication scheme using two UART ports and two active‑HIGH relay modules driving 12 V electromagnetic door locks, with the first lock’s relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) and the second to GPIO27 (BCM); the program must read 6‑digit codes from /dev/serial0 (primary UART on GPIO14/15) and /dev/serial1 (secondary UART) at 9600 baud, 8N1 framing, using a 5‑second per‑port read timeout and non‑blocking reads in a single main loop so the codes may arrive in any order, resetting the input buffer on any non‑digit character, and only when both received codes match each other and also match the constant expected code “123456” (using a constant‑time string comparison to avoid timing side‑channels) should it drive both relay GPIOs HIGH for exactly 2 seconds via the library’s API call and then set them LOW; the code must detect and log to stderr any failure to initialize the driver library, any failure to open the UART ports via the library’s API call, any read timeout reported by the library’s API call, and any GPIO write failure, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that perform a clean shutdown by forcing both lock relays LOW (locked), closing the library’s API call handles, and invoking the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor on the physical GPIO4 line via the GPIO bus, polls the sensor every 50 ms, and when a motion event (PIR HIGH) is detected logs a syslog entry, activates a door‑strike relay on physical GPIO17 for exactly 1 second while logging the relay on/off events, then de‑energizes the relay; if the PIR signal remains continuously HIGH for more than 10 seconds the program must trigger a failsafe that de‑energizes the relay, logs a LOG_WARNING entry describing a potential malfunction, and also logs a shutdown event, and in all cases every driver library call must be checked for errors and any failure reported to the system journal via syslog(3); the implementation must open the driver’s API call by name and request the two GPIO lines explicitly using the modern driver API calls, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown that releases all GPIO lines, closes the chip, closes the log, ensures the relay is driven LOW before releasing the line, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that runs a timed sequential irrigation cycle across a 4‑channel active‑LOW relay module connected on the GPIO bus, with relay 1 on GPIO4 (BCM), relay 2 on GPIO17 (BCM), relay 3 on GPIO27 (BCM) and relay 4 on GPIO22 (BCM); the program must initialize all relays to OFF (set HIGH) at startup, then use a single timer (timer 0) that fires every 60 seconds to drive an internal state machine that activates each relay for 5 minutes (300 seconds) in order, inserts a 1‑minute (60 seconds) pause between activations, and loops back to the first relay after the fourth, logging every state change to syslog with timestamps and the identifier “irrigation_system”, checking every the driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call) and logging any failure to syslog before exiting cleanly, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM by deactivating all relays (setting them HIGH), releasing GPIO resources via the library's API call(), closing syslog, and exiting, while the main loop is a sleep loop that checks a volatile sig_atomic_t flag.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a GPIO‑connected HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor (TRIG on GPIO4 BCM, ECHO on GPIO18 BCM) to measure distance in an interrupt‑driven fashion and log each valid reading to a file named distance_log.txt in CSV format “timestamp_ns,distance_cm”, running indefinitely; the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse on the TRIG line, wait 200 ms between trigger cycles, capture the echo pulse width with rising‑edge and falling‑edge interrupt callbacks protected by a mutex, discard any measurement whose pulse width exceeds 23 200 µs (approximately 4 m, the sensor’s maximum range), treat a missing echo within 100 ms after a trigger as a timeout error, handle driver library initialization failure, file open failure, invalid pulse widths and sensor timeouts, record timestamps with nanosecond precision using a 32‑bit tick counter that wraps roughly every 71.6 minutes, and install a SIGINT handler that on termination cancels the callbacks, closes the log file, terminates the driver library and destroys the mutex.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads the Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, detects a free‑fall when the measured acceleration magnitude falls below 0.2 g, then detects an impact when the magnitude rises above 1.5 g (allowing the free‑fall and impact thresholds to be overridden by optional command‑line arguments), and upon detecting the impact activates a buzzer connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for exactly one second; the implementation must initialize the I2C interface and the sensor driver with full error checking, retry any I2C communication failure up to three times, handle the absence of the sensor or bus errors gracefully, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT the program performs a clean shutdown releasing all resources and leaving the GPIO and I2C bus in a safe state.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the GPIO bus to drive two 28BYJ‑48 stepper motors with ULN2003 driver boards, configuring Motor 1 (X‑axis) IN1 on GPIO4 (BCM), IN2 on GPIO17 (BCM), IN3 on GPIO27 (BCM) and IN4 on GPIO22 (BCM), and Motor 2 (Y‑axis) IN1 on GPIO5 (BCM), IN2 on GPIO6 (BCM), IN3 on GPIO13 (BCM) and IN4 on GPIO19 (BCM) as outputs, employing a 4‑step wave drive sequence (single‑coil excitation) with a 1000 µs step delay, calculating the required steps from the 28BYJ‑48’s 1/64 gear ratio and 2048 steps per revolution to trace a 50 mm square, checking that the driver initialization succeeds and verifying each API call, handling any motor movement failures gracefully, and installing a SIGINT handler that safely stops both motors, sets all GPIO pins low and releases resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer on the I2C bus, reading acceleration at a 10 Hz interval (every 100 ms) and configuring the sensor for a ±2 g range, high‑resolution 12‑bit left‑justified mode with a 100 Hz output data rate, supporting only a single sensor; the program must accept optional command‑line arguments “‑a” for the I2C address in hex and “‑t” for a threshold in g (default 2.0 g, must be > 0), validate that the address falls within the documented range, and on any axis exceeding the threshold log a line containing a timestamp and the three axis values to /var/log/high_acceleration.log before invoking “sudo shutdown -h now”; it must handle I2C open or configuration errors by performing cleanup (closing the bus and terminating the driver library) and exiting with code 0 in non‑hardware environments, handle sensor read errors by returning zeros and continuing, use the library’s API calls for I2C operations and single‑byte register writes (which return 0 on success), and install a SIGINT handler that gracefully terminates by closing I2C and shutting down the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements an autonomous line‑following robot using a SunFounder 3‑Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) connected on the GPIO bus, with the left sensor wired to GPIO4 (BCM), the center sensor to GPIO17 (BCM), the right sensor to GPIO27 (BCM) and an active‑high alert LED/buzzer on GPIO22 (BCM); the program must poll the three sensor pins every 10 ms, log each reading (left, center, right) into a circular buffer of size five, check all driver library initialization and line‑request return values and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, drive the alert pin HIGH for 2 seconds when the center sensor reports “no line” (logic 1) for five consecutive readings, otherwise move forward when the center detects a line (logic 0), turn left when the left sensor detects a line, turn right when the right sensor detects a line, and stop when all sensors read “no line”, using placeholder motor control functions, and ensure that on any exit path triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads magnetic field data from a Silicon Labs Si7210 I2C Hall effect sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, samples every 100 ms, and triggers a relay connected to GPIO 17 (BCM, active high) whenever the field exceeds a threshold of 5.0 mT, while appending timestamped entries in ISO 8601 format (YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS) to magnetic_events.txt for each reading, each relay state change, and any error; the program must check every the driver library call: the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call; if the library's API call fails, log the error and exit; on a read/write failure, log the error, deactivate the relay, and retry on the next cycle; if register the documented value does not clear after 50 poll attempts, log a timeout error and skip the cycle; a SIGINT handler must close the I2C handle, deactivate the relay, terminate the driver library, and log the shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus with BCM numbering to control a KY‑019 relay module connected to GPIO 18, listening on TCP port 5000 for case‑insensitive commands “ON” and “OFF” (trailing whitespace must be ignored), invoking the library’s API call to switch the relay and logging every activation, deactivation, and any invalid‑command event with a timestamp to a file named relay_log.txt; the implementation must include comprehensive error handling for all socket operations (creation, bind, listen, accept, and read) as well as for GPIO initialization, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that gracefully shut down the library’s API call, close the sockets and the log file, turn off the relay, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors two Sensirion SLF3S‑1300F liquid‑flow sensors (40 ml/min version) connected to I2C bus 1, using the documented I2C addresses for sensor 1 and sensor 2, and controls a safety relay on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering, active‑high) with a 100 ms polling loop; each iteration must read three bytes from each sensor, validate the CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial, initial value and no final XOR, and if a read returns fewer than three bytes or the CRC check fails, a warning is written to stderr and the cycle is skipped without changing the relay state, otherwise the flow rates are logged with millisecond timestamps to flow_log.txt in append mode with an immediate flush, and if both reads succeed and either sensor reports a flow below 5.0 ml/min the relay is energized (write 1) and otherwise de‑energized (write 0) when both are at or above 5.0 ml/min; the program must check the library’s API return codes for opening I2C bus 1 with flags 0 for each sensor, verify that the start‑measurement command write (the documented two‑byte sequence) returns 0 for each sensor, and also verify the GPIO 18 configuration call’s return code, performing full cleanup of any partially‑initialized resources on any failure, and on shutdown triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM it must de‑energize the relay, close any open I2C handles, call the library’s cleanup function, and print a shutdown message, while compiling cleanly with gcc ‑Wall ‑Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors the Seeed Studio Rain Sensor v1.0 digital output on GPIO 17 (BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑up, polling every 200 ms over the GPIO bus, and drives a DC motor window actuator through an L298N driver using ENA on GPIO 22 (BCM), IN1 on GPIO 23 (BCM) and IN2 on GPIO 24 (BCM); the sensor pulls its DO pin low when rain is present and high when dry, so the program must detect a rising‑edge (dry‑to‑wet transition) and, on that edge only, start the close‑window sequence by setting ENA high, IN1 high, IN2 low, holding the motor for exactly 5 seconds using the library’s API call() or usleep() (no busy‑wait), then stopping the motor by setting ENA low and both IN1 and IN2 low while verifying each call, logging all events with syslog (facility LOG_USER, identifier “rain_window”) as LOG_INFO for startup, rain detection, motor start/stop and shutdown and using LOG_ERR or LOG_WARNING for any call failures, suppressing further triggers until the sensor reads dry for at least three consecutive polls (≈600 ms), and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that stops the motor (all calls LOW), calls the library’s API call() to clean up, closes syslog and exits cleanly, with every library API call return checked and logged, all within a single‑process design without forks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to control a hobby servo acting as a door‑lock actuator based on two momentary push‑buttons, with the servo connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18), the lock button to GPIO 21 (BCM) and the unlock button to GPIO 22 (BCM), both buttons wired to ground when pressed and therefore requiring internal pull‑up resistors to be enabled; the program must poll the buttons in a tight loop with a small sleep to keep CPU usage low, implement debouncing by waiting for the button release plus a short delay so that a single press is not registered multiple times, drive the library’s API call() with a 2000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 21 button is pressed to lock, a 1000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 22 button is pressed to unlock, and output status messages to stdout for lock, unlock, and shutdown events, verify that the API call() returns success for both pulse‑width commands and exit with an error message on failure, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that stops the servo by sending a pulse width of 0, calls the API call() one final time, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a PIR motion sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, BCM 4) using a 100 ms polling interval and, on each rising edge, activates a relay‑controlled 12 V LED floodlight connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM 17) for exactly 60 seconds before turning it off, while appending activation events with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and deactivation events with a timestamp and the measured duration in seconds to a file named security_log.txt; the program must verify that the driver library is successfully initialized, check the return code of every library API call as well as the result of every fopen, fprintf and fclose operation, and if any file operation fails it must turn off the floodlight before exiting, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly turns off the floodlight, releases the driver library resources, and exits with code 0, ensuring that the floodlight is OFF on all exit paths and that no driver library is used directly in the code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) to toggle a relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) only on a fresh rising‑edge touch of electrode 0, applying a 200 ms debounce to that electrode, performing a full MPR121 initialization that includes a soft‑reset, configuration of baseline filtering (MHD, NHD, NCL, FDL) to the documented values, setting the debounce to the documented value, configuring FFI, SFI and CDT to the documented values, enabling auto‑config with the documented range, and enabling exactly 12 electrodes as documented; the program must set the relay to a known OFF state at startup and also ensure it is OFF on shutdown, must implement robust error handling for every driver library and I2C call by checking return values and handling sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the GPIO bus to control a servo motor on BCM GPIO17 and read a PIR sensor on BCM GPIO4, listening for TCP connections on port 5000; the program must accept commands of the form “the library's API call <angle>” where <angle> is 0‑180 and generate a software PWM signal at 50 Hz with a 1‑2 ms pulse width to position the servo, and also respond to the command “PIR” by sending back “PIR:0” or “PIR:1” over the socket, while logging all events, commands, and errors to both syslog (LOG_USER facility) and a file named security.log with ISO 8601 timestamps, checking the result of every driver library call, socket syscall, and file I/O operation and, if GPIO initialization fails, logging the error and exiting with a non‑zero status; the code must include <stdarg.h> for variadic functions so it compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources, closes the socket and the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads ambient light from a BH1750 sensor on I2C1 (GPIO2 =SDA, GPIO3 =SCL) using the documented address, waiting at least 120 ms after each trigger before reading the 2‑byte lux result and sampling every 2 seconds, logs a timestamp and the lux value to grow_log.txt, and drives a grow‑light relay on GPIO23 (BCM) so that the relay is activated when the lux reading falls below 150 and deactivated when it is 150 or above, while implementing robust error handling that checks the return codes of every I2C call and of file operations, logs any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions and simply retries on the next cycle, and ensures that on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—the program cleanly releases all resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, deactivating the relay, and invoking the appropriate library cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors weight using a TAL220B load cell with an HX711 amplifier over a bit‑banged GPIO bus, reading HX711 DOUT on GPIO23 (physical pin 16) and HX711 SCK on GPIO24 (physical pin 18), and drives a solenoid lock on GPIO25 (physical pin 22); the program must perform a startup tare by averaging ten 24‑bit two’s‑complement readings (obtained by waiting for DOUT to go LOW, clocking out 24 bits MSB‑first, then one extra clock pulse to select Channel A gain 128), then in the main loop poll the weight every 500 ms, averaging five readings per measurement cycle, apply an optional scale factor, and if the measured weight exceeds a threshold (default 1000 grams, overridable with a --threshold <grams> command‑line argument) activate the solenoid lock by setting GPIO25 HIGH for 200 ms before returning it LOW; each HX711 read must check that DOUT goes LOW within 1 second, logging an error via syslog and retrying up to three times before exiting, and every driver call must be verified for errors; the program should accept optional --scale <factor> and --duration <ms> arguments, log informational and error messages through syslog, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO lines and chips, closes syslog, and ensures the solenoid is set LOW before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS that controls a relay module attached to the GPIO bus on GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) by subscribing to the MQTT topic home/lights/control with QoS 0, connecting to a broker at localhost port 1883 using client ID relay_controller_1 and a clean session, maintaining a 60‑second keep‑alive, and on successful connect logging the event to syslog (facility LOG_USER, tag mqtt_relay) and subscribing to the topic; the program must initialize the GPIO driver, configure GPIO17 as an output and drive it LOW (relay OFF) at startup, then in the main thread run the MQTT client loop, handling incoming payloads as NUL‑terminated strings where the exact values “ON” set GPIO17 HIGH (relay energized) and “OFF” set it LOW (relay de‑energized), logging any empty or invalid payload as an error (syslog LOG_ERR) without changing the relay state, and for every connection, subscription, disconnection, or error event logging the details to syslog, checking all return codes from the driver and MQTT client and reporting failures via syslog while never exiting on transient MQTT errors; on loop errors or unexpected disconnects the program must wait five seconds before attempting to reconnect, and a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must stop the loop, set GPIO17 LOW, disconnect and destroy the MQTT client, clean up the driver library, call the library cleanup function, and close the syslog; the source should be compiled with gcc using optimization level 2 and all warnings enabled, producing an executable named relay_controller.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that moves five hobby servos connected to the GPIO bus to predefined positions by generating a 50 Hz PWM signal (20 ms period) on BCM GPIO 7 for Servo 1, BCM GPIO 8 for Servo 2, BCM GPIO 9 for Servo 3, BCM GPIO 10 for Servo 4, and BCM GPIO 11 for Servo 5, holding each pulse for three seconds; the program must initialize the driver library and verify the return code before use, then output pulse widths constrained between 500 µs and 2500 µs with target values of 1000 µs, 1500 µs, 2000 µs, 500 µs, and 2500 µs respectively for the five servos, and finally cleanly stop the PWM and release all library resources before exiting.
